extracted.intended_audience: college faculty, program directors, and administrators implementing or assessing quantitative literacy / Math Across the Curriculum programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and assessment practices for designing, implementing, and evaluating Math Across the Curriculum / quantitative literacy programs in higher education, including surveys, competency exams, tutoring centers, curricular examples, and faculty development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre/post attitude surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Administer student attitude surveys at the beginning and end of the academic quarter to monitor changes in student attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a five-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Agree to 5 = Strongly Disagree). Collect demographic and tracking information on the survey back. Analyze paired pre/post data to detect shifts in attitudes (report means, effect sizes, and p-values). Note that causation cannot be established from such data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Likert mean shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret average shifts on the Likert scale so that a lower mean indicates greater agreement with the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report pre and post means and statistical significance (e.g., p-values). Indicate when changes move in a 'positive' or 'undesirable' direction (the paper flags statement #35 as undesirable despite a shift).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze subgroup (gender) differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Disaggregate attitude-change analyses by gender (and other groups) to identify statistically significant shifts that differ between subgroups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report pre/post means and significance separately for men and women; interpret differences in context (e.g., improvements in confidence or reductions in anxiety for women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report effect sizes and statistical significance
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting survey or assessment results, report effect sizes and p-values for reported changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List items showing small effect sizes or statistically significant shifts; include exact p thresholds (e.g., p < .001, p < .01, p < .05) to indicate strength of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty development assessment (qualitative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather qualitative data from faculty participants to assess the project's effect on faculty teaching in MAC courses and generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews or qualitative assessments (e.g., Dr. Rob Cole's work) to capture impacts on instructors' teaching practice and curricular changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quantitative learning a shared responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the program so that improving students' quantitative skills and attitudes is a shared responsibility across disciplines (modeled on Writing Across the Curriculum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cooperation of faculty in other disciplines; use institutional incentives (e.g., NSF support, core curriculum commitment) to foster buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set realistic, course-specific goals: skill vs. attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between improving skill and improving attitude and set course-appropriate goals (some courses aim for skill improvement, others for attitude change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that an art course may reasonably target attitude/awareness rather than algebraic skill; physics might aim for algebra skill gains. Tailor interventions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select accessible, discipline-appropriate applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose mathematical applications that are accessible and appropriate to the discipline and instructor comfort level (e.g., fractals in an art class rather than quadratic equations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find examples that fit naturally into the existing curriculum and that faculty feel comfortable teaching; student engagement and enjoyment are important indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make students aware when they are using math
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly point out to students when an activity involves mathematics so they recognize the application and its relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syllabus notes, cross-course references, and in-class reminders (e.g., linking MATH120 material to Geography 103 or Psychology 101) to raise 'math awareness'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and share cross-referenced, course-specific examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect examples showing how math is used in specific core courses and compile them in a booklet or resource with cross-references for instructors and students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List examples by course number and use them in syllabi to demonstrate payoff and relevance of math across students' college experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency exam: faculty consultation and course relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Design each math competency exam in consultation with the non-math course instructor so the exam covers only necessary skills for success in that specific course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating a 'wish list' of skills; focus on what students will actually need in exams, labs, or assignments for the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency exam: test only necessary, basic topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit competency exams to basic math that students should reasonably be expected to have already learned (not pushing beyond prerequisites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics should be diagnostic of readiness (examples include algebra fundamentals) and not be so long or difficult as to seem onerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency exam: timing and logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Administer the first competency test in class during the first week, grade it, and return it by the next class meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-testing should be done outside class (e.g., in the Math Center) to avoid consuming class time and instructor grading load; this helps secure instructor buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency exam: remedial as well as diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the testing program remedial as well as diagnostic — allow students to receive help and re-take tests until they pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set a passing score (often near mastery, e.g., ~80%). Provide opportunities for re-testing with different forms and offer Math Center support for remediation and learning rather than punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use re-testing as a learning opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold re-testing in a learning center where staff can go over the test with students so that re-testing becomes an instructional process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Math Center staff should review mistakes with students; re-testing on a drop-in basis helps remediation and reduces burden on course instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide incentives to motivate remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Include incentives (grade consequences or bonus points) to encourage students to correct deficiencies and retake competency tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without incentives, many students will not take initiative to remediate after a poor diagnostic score; instructors can require passing by a deadline or award bonus points for timely completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gateway testing policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use competency tests as 'gateway' requirements where students must pass by a specified date to complete the course or to earn other benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courses require passing by a deadline to continue; other instructors give bonus points for early completion — policies are set by the instructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math Center as hub for support and assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a Math Center to support curricular integration: provide computer labs, peer tutors, re-testing, grading assistance, and faculty consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff the center with qualified peer tutors from relevant disciplines, supervise them carefully, and use the center for drop-in tutoring, re-testing, and collaborating with instructors on competency exams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of non-credit tutorial (Hamilton model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer a self-paced, tutor-based, non-credit tutorial as one option to fulfill quantitative literacy requirements, aimed at students avoiding math courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the tutorial grade-free, supported by trained peer tutors acting as mentors, and structured to build transferable 'life skills' (banking, nutrition, finance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core modules for non-credit tutorial
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the non-credit tutorial around core modules: I. Basic Computation, II. Algebraic Expressions, III. Graphs and Charts, IV. Proportional & Functional Reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose modules to be relevant and challenging yet accessible to 'math phobic' students; note that some topics (e.g., counting and probability) may be omitted intentionally.
